vignette:
He is a 61-year-old North American man who has spent most of his working life behind the wheel, and for years he thought the steadiness of the bus route suited him. He liked the rhythm of it, the familiar stops, the same intersections each morning, the small talk with regular passengers, the sense that he knew how to keep moving even when life was complicated. That faith in routine changes after he is taken captive and tortured, an experience he still describes in fragments, as if the mind can only bring forward pieces at a time.

He remembers the beginning clearly: the sudden loss of control, the confinement, the first realization that no appeal, no explanation, no ordinary decency will matter. In the days that follow, time becomes distorted. He learns to measure life in sounds of doors opening, footsteps approaching, the smell of sweat and metal, the anticipation before pain. He says that what stays with him most is not one single blow but the helplessness of waiting for the next one. Even now, he can feel his body brace when he talks about it, his shoulders lifting, his hands tightening as if they are again trying to protect himself.

After he is released, he returns home physically changed and emotionally unfamiliar to himself. His wife is relieved to have him back, but he cannot settle into the comfort of the home they once shared. He sleeps lightly and poorly, waking at the smallest noise. At night he lies awake listening to the house, scanning for threats in the dark. He avoids being touched unexpectedly, especially from behind, and he dislikes having doors closed in ways that limit his view of an exit. He does not call these reactions fear; he says he is simply paying attention, but his body remains on alert long after there is any objective danger.

Driving, once automatic, becomes difficult in new ways. He continues working because he needs to, and because he wants to keep proving to himself that he is still the man who can handle a route, a schedule, a crowd. But the bus now feels like a place where he is responsible for everyone and vulnerable himself. If a passenger raises a voice, if a motorcycle swerves too close, if he is boxed in by traffic, his mind flashes back with alarming speed. He grips the steering wheel hard enough to ache. Sometimes he has to slow down just to breathe through a wave of panic, though he is embarrassed to admit that he experiences it at all. He becomes more cautious, more irritable, and more exhausted by the end of the day than he used to be.

He is haunted by memories that arrive without permission. A sound, a smell, a certain kind of silence can pull him back instantly. He may be standing in the kitchen or waiting at a stoplight when he is suddenly elsewhere, flooded by images he does not want. At other times he feels strangely absent, as if he is watching his life from a short distance away. He avoids stories about war, captivity, or abuse on the news because they quickly unmoor him. He no longer enjoys social gatherings in the way he once did, partly because he feels out of place and partly because he is always monitoring himself, worried he will seem shaky or angry or not fully present.

He notices that he is less patient with his wife and grandchildren than he wants to be. He loves them, but he keeps his emotions guarded, and when they ask what happened to him, he gives brief answers or changes the subject. He carries guilt that he survived and returned when others did not, though he rarely speaks of this openly. Some mornings he wakes already tired, with a heaviness in his chest and a sense that the day will require more strength than he has. Yet he still gets dressed, still checks the bus, still completes his route. He insists on doing what needs to be done, even on the days when the past feels closer than the present and his body seems to remember danger before his mind can remind it that he is home.
